name: Torsemide

card.summary: A prescription loop diuretic for heart-failure fluid overload; mentioned in depuffing circles but never studied for appearance.
card.note: Prescription loop diuretic; can cause dehydration and electrolyte loss.

quick.overview:
Torsemide (torasemide) is a loop diuretic prescribed for fluid buildup from heart failure, kidney disease and liver disease.

It appears in this wiki because loop diuretics are discussed as water pills in depuffing communities. No published study has tested it for facial puffiness or any appearance purpose.
quick.mechanism: Like other loop diuretics it reduces sodium reabsorption in the kidney so more salt and water leave in the urine. Compared with furosemide it has higher oral bioavailability (about 80-90%) and a longer effect at equivalent doses.[1][5]
quick.risks: Reported effects include headache, increased urination, diarrhea, cough and dizziness; low potassium and hearing loss are less common. Wikipedia advises against use in pregnancy and breastfeeding. It is a prescription drug.[1]

lead: Torsemide, also spelled torasemide, is a prescription loop diuretic and sulfonamide used mainly to relieve fluid accumulation from heart failure, kidney disease and liver disease. It can be given orally or intravenously and is sold under names such as Demadex.[1][2]

In depuffing and water-weight discussions, loop diuretics are named as drugs that make the body shed water and sodium. People who describe using them aim for a leaner, less swollen face and body. The effect is a loss of fluid, not fat, and the drugs are prescription-controlled because of effects on blood pressure, kidney function and electrolytes.[2]

It was patented in 1974 and entered medical use in 1993, and it is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1] Trials have compared it with furosemide in heart failure; the large TRANSFORM-HF trial reported no significant difference in all-cause mortality between the two.[3] No published research has examined torsemide for cosmetic purposes such as facial depuffing.

paras: Torsemide is used to treat fluid overload in heart failure and is sometimes used for high blood pressure, although it is a less preferred option there.[1] The US label lists edema associated with heart failure, renal disease and hepatic disease, and hypertension.[2]

Research has also looked at it in other fluid-related settings: a 2025 meta-analysis reviewed postpartum diuretics for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, a 118-patient phase 2 trial registered torsemide for postpartum hypertension, and a 2026 randomised trial compared torsemide with furosemide for oedema in children with nephrotic syndrome.[14][10][6] A torsemide solution was conditionally approved by the US FDA in May 2024 for dogs with heart failure.[1]

A 2001 open-label randomised trial of 234 patients with chronic heart failure compared torsemide with furosemide, motivated by furosemide's erratic oral absorption.[4] The pragmatic TRANSFORM-HF randomised trial, which enrolled 2,859 patients at 60 US hospitals after a heart-failure hospitalisation, reported no significant difference in all-cause mortality between torsemide and furosemide.[3] Analyses across the ejection-fraction spectrum were published in 2024.[7]

Wikipedia describes earlier and smaller analyses as linking torsemide to fewer rehospitalisations and better functional class than furosemide.[1] Reviews of loop diuretic choice discuss torsemide's pharmacological advantages alongside the shortage of large outcome trials before TRANSFORM-HF.[12][13] A 1993 six-week study in congestive heart failure and a 1993 review in hypertension are among its earlier clinical reports.[8][9]

Headache, frequent urination, diarrhea, cough and dizziness are described as common, while hearing loss and low potassium are less common. Wikipedia states that no evidence shows torsemide causes ototoxicity in humans, and notes that loop diuretics may deplete thiamine with long-term use.[1]

The US label lists excessive urination as the most common adverse reaction (6.7%) and warns of hypotension and worsening renal function, electrolyte and metabolic abnormalities, and ototoxicity; it notes that excessive diuresis may cause symptomatic dehydration, volume reduction and acute kidney injury, particularly in salt-depleted patients or those on renin-angiotensin inhibitors.[2] There are no human pregnancy data on the label, and Wikipedia advises against use in pregnancy and breastfeeding.[1][2]

Torsemide acts in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, where it inhibits the Na+/K+/2Cl- carrier, raising urinary excretion of sodium, chloride and water.[2] Diuretic activity correlates better with the rate of drug excretion in urine than with blood concentration.[2]

Oral bioavailability is roughly 80-90%, protein binding exceeds 99%, and about 80% is metabolised in the liver.[1] In a randomised crossover trial of 16 patients with compensated heart failure, torsemide was absorbed faster than furosemide (time to peak about 1.1 versus 2.4 hours).[5] Wikipedia describes a longer diuretic effect at equivalent doses and relatively less potassium loss than furosemide.[1]
Torsemide is a sulfonamide and pyridine-based compound with formula C16H20N4O3S and molar mass of about 348 g/mol; Wikipedia gives the INN as torasemide and the USAN as torsemide.[1]

Torsemide is prescription-only and is available as a generic; Wikipedia reports it was the 193rd most commonly prescribed drug in the US in 2023.[1] It is listed among loop diuretics discussed as gray-market water pills in looksmaxxing and depuffing contexts, though sources contain little substantive community discussion of torsemide specifically. Brand names include Demadex, Tortas and Wator, and the INN (torasemide) and USAN (torsemide) spellings both appear in the literature.[1]

No studies found on torsemide for facial depuffing or other appearance goals. Trials in heart failure include TRANSFORM-HF (about 2,900 participants) and an open-label comparison with furosemide in 234 patients.[3][4][15] A 47-patient phase 3 trial comparing torsemide with furosemide in stable heart failure is registered, as are bioavailability studies of immediate- and extended-release tablets.[11] Torsemide has also been studied for hypertension, for postpartum hypertension and for oedema in paediatric nephrotic syndrome.[9][10][6]

timeline.event: Enters medical use; early clinical studies in heart failure and hypertension published.[1][8][9]
Randomised crossover pharmacokinetic comparison with furosemide published.[5]
Open-label randomised trial versus furosemide in 234 heart-failure patients.[4]
US FDA conditionally approves a torsemide solution for dogs with heart failure.[1]

lore.intro: Torsemide is mentioned only rarely in depuffing and water-weight discussions, typically as one of several loop diuretics.

claims.claim: Loop diuretics like torsemide can flush excess water to reduce puffiness.
claims.believers: Proponents of diuretic use for a leaner or less puffy look describe water loss as the mechanism behind a drier, less swollen appearance.
claims.experts: The drug label describes increased excretion of sodium, chloride and water and warns of dehydration, low blood pressure, electrolyte disturbance and kidney effects; no published study has tested facial puffiness.[2]

chain: Blocks sodium and chloride reabsorption in the loop of Henle
More sodium and water leave in urine
Less fluid held in tissue, which users associate with a less puffy look
angle.text: Loop diuretics reduce fluid volume, which is why they are mentioned in depuffing circles as water pills. Torsemide itself has been studied in clinical settings for edema, not for facial appearance.
